title: Star Watch: Meteor shower, planetary pairings, and darker skies this week

content:
(WJHL) — November is kicking off with plenty of opportunities for skywatchers across Northeast Tennessee and Southwest Virginia, including a meteor shower known for its bright fireballs, close encounters between planets and the Moon, and darker nights that could make stargazing even better.

One of the first astronomical highlights of the month arrives Wednesday night into Thursday morning as the Southern Taurid meteor shower reaches its peak.

Unlike some meteor showers that produce dozens of shooting stars per hour, the Southern Taurids typically produce only around five meteors per hour under ideal viewing conditions.

However, what the shower lacks in quantity, it can make up for in brightness.

The Taurids are known for producing fireballs, exceptionally bright meteors that can illuminate the night sky for several seconds.

For the best chance of spotting one, skywatchers should head somewhere away from city lights and look toward the sky late Wednesday night into the early morning hours Thursday.

Early risers will also have something to look forward to Tuesday morning, November 3.

A waning crescent Moon will appear close to Regulus, the brightest star in the constellation Leo, with Jupiter shining nearby.

Mars will also be visible in the morning sky, giving skywatchers several celestial objects to look for before sunrise.

The grouping will be visible toward the eastern and southeastern sky, with the hours before daybreak offering a good viewing opportunity across the Tri-Cities.

No telescope is necessary to enjoy the display.

Throughout the week, the Moon will continue transitioning into its waning crescent phase as it approaches the next new moon on Monday, November 9.

With less of the Moon illuminated each night, there will be less moonlight washing out fainter stars and other objects in the night sky.

That could make the second half of the week particularly favorable for stargazing, especially in rural areas of Northeast Tennessee and Southwest Virginia where light pollution is limited.

The darker conditions could also help skywatchers catch a glimpse of meteors associated with the ongoing Taurid meteor showers.

Another celestial gathering will take place Saturday morning, November 7, when a very thin crescent Moon appears close to Venus.

The bright star Spica, located in the constellation Virgo, will also appear nearby, creating a striking grouping low in the east-southeastern sky.

Venus is one of the brightest objects in the sky, making it relatively easy to identify without a telescope.

For Tri-Cities viewers, the best opportunity to catch the gathering will be around 6 a.m. EST, before sunrise.

An unobstructed view of the eastern horizon will be important, as the objects will appear relatively low in the sky.

As always, cloud cover and local weather conditions will play an important role in determining how much of this week's celestial activity will be visible across the region.

For the best viewing experience, find a location away from bright lights, allow your eyes time to adjust to the darkness and keep an eye on the latest forecast.

Happy star watching!
